figures.finding: In the 100 top-grossing North American films of 2024, 33.6% of speaking or named characters were female, 66.2% male and 0.18% non-binary (4,401 characters), while 55% of films had a female lead or co-lead.
figures.applies: US/North American theatrical film, top 100 domestic-grossing narrative films, release year 2024 (series 2007-2024).
figures.use: A US feature film's speaking parts are drawn about one in three for an Actress and two in three for an Actor, while the lead is written for an Actress in about half of films.

sources.said: Gender. 4,401 speaking or named characters were coded across the 100 top-grossing movies of 2024. Of these characters, 66.2% were male, 33.6% were female, and <1% (.18) were non-binary.
The percentage of films with a female protagonist (lead/co lead) was at a historic high in 2024 (55%).

figures.finding: In the 100 top-grossing US films of 2025, females were 38% of speaking characters and 36% of major characters.
figures.applies: US theatrical film, top 100 domestic-grossing films of 2025 (as ranked by The Numbers).
figures.use: Cross-check for the US film share: a second, independent count gives 38% of speaking parts to actresses in 2025.

sources.said: The percentage of female characters in speaking roles increased slightly to 38% in 2025, up 1 percentage point from 37% in 2024. The percentage of major female characters declined 3 percentage points, from 39% in 2024 to 36% in 2025.

figures.finding: In US prime-time broadcast and streaming series of 2025-26, females were 44.2% of speaking characters (46.3% on broadcast networks, 43.0% on streaming), males 55.7%, transgender characters 0.1%.
figures.applies: US original dramas, comedies and reality programmes on the five broadcast networks and eight streaming services, August 2025 to June 2026 (one random episode per series).
figures.use: A US television series writes its speaking parts closer to even (about 44 actress parts in 100) than a US feature film does.

sources.said: In 2025-26, females accounted for 44% (44.2%) of all speaking characters on broadcast network and streaming programs. This represents a decline of 2 percentage points from 46% in 2024-2025. Males comprised 56% (55.7%), and transgender characters less than one half of 1% (0.1%) of speaking characters
In 2025-26, females comprised 46% (46.3%) of all speaking characters appearing on broadcast network programs.
In 2025-26, females accounted for 43% (43.0%) of all speaking characters on streaming programs.

figures.finding: In 2025 streaming films from the major US streamers, women were 58.4% of leads but 42.7% of all actors.
figures.applies: US streaming films released in 2025 by the major streamers (89 films with leads coded).
figures.use: A streaming feature's lead is written for an Actress somewhat more often than for an Actor, while its whole cast still leans to actors.

sources.said: Women exceeded proportionate representation among streaming film leads (58.4 percent).
Less than proportionate representation among total streaming film actors (42.7 percent)

figures.finding: Of 3,714 character breakdowns for 269 SAG-AFTRA television shows (January to August 2017), 57.6% were written for men, 37.9% for women, 4.4% open gender and 0.1% gender queer or non-binary.
figures.applies: US scripted English-language television (broadcast, cable, streaming), breakdowns distributed January-August 2017.
figures.use: A breakdown carries a gender: about 58 in 100 US TV breakdowns are open to an Actor only, 38 to an Actress only, and about 4 to either, so Billed As decides which of them reach the player.

sources.said: Figure 1 shows the gender distribution in the Breakdowns as Men 57.6% (n = 2,141), Women 37.9% (n = 1,408), Open Gender
Open Gender means casting is open to either a man or woman in the role.

figures.finding: Of all US feature-film breakdowns from 1 June to 31 August 2006, 94% designated a sex: 59% male and 35% female.
figures.applies: US feature films, every breakdown (stunts and extras excluded), June-August 2006.
figures.use: An older film-only count that agrees with the TV count: nearly every breakdown names a sex, about three in five for men.

sources.said: Ninety-four percent of the roles in the breakdown sample contained sex designations. Fifty-nine percent of the roles were designated male roles, and 35% were designated female.

figures.finding: SAG's Casting Data Reports, compiled from producers' hiring data under the TV/Theatrical contracts, found men cast in twice as many roles as women, a 2 to 1 ratio steady from 2006 to 2008.
figures.applies: US film and television roles under SAG's TV/Theatrical contracts, 2006-2008.
figures.use: The union's own count (the last published) confirms the film and television split: two Actor parts to every Actress part.

sources.said: continue to be cast in twice the number of roles. The2 to 1 ratio has held steady since 2006.

figures.finding: In UK television (programmes broadcast 1 April 2025 to 31 March 2026), women made 52% of scripted on-screen contributions, 49% of non-scripted and 49.6% of all on-screen contributions.
figures.applies: UK television monitored by Diamond, 2025 reporting year.
figures.use: UK scripted television, counted by actors cast, is at parity: an Actress meets about as many UK TV parts as an Actor.

sources.said: However, women are less well represented in non-scripted roles (49%) compared to scripted roles (52%)
They made 49.6% of on-screen contributions in 2025, a decrease from 52% of contributions in 2021, and slightly lower than population estimates (51% Annual Population Survey ).
It is important to note that in scripted roles, the data relates to the actors playing a role and not the characters they portray.

figures.finding: Main characters in Australian TV drama broadcast 2016-2021 were split evenly, 50% women and 50% men, with 0.2% non-binary.
figures.applies: Australian TV drama (broadcast, subscription and streaming), main characters, 2016-2021.
figures.use: Australian TV drama's main parts are written half for an Actress and half for an Actor.

sources.said: the gender of main characters was evenly split between women and men (50% of characters), similar to the split of women and men in the Australian population.
Our study found five characters whose gender identity was non‑binary (0.2%)

figures.finding: Canadian broadcasting in 2016: women held 37% of all speaking roles and 40% in English-language dramas (Nordicity for the CRTC, as Screen Australia reports it).
figures.applies: Canadian television programming, 2016 study (3,109 speaking roles in 196 programmes).
figures.use: Canada's home-market share: about 37 in 100 speaking parts for an Actress (2016, the latest published count found).

sources.said: Nordicity’s 2016 study of Canadian broadcasting found women held just 37% of all speaking roles, including 40% in English language dramas but strong representation in English language children’s dramas (63%).

figures.finding: On US Equity stage contracts in 2023, men received 44.4% and women 43.2% of new contracts, and non-binary or third-gender members 1.6%.
figures.applies: US professional stage (Actors' Equity Association), new contracts in 2023 across principal actors, chorus and stage managers; gender is self-reported and many members did not answer.
figures.use: Stage work is near parity between Actor and Actress, unlike film.

sources.said: We are moving closer to parity amongst both men and women regarding percentage of new contracts (44.4% and 43.2% in 2023 respectively), but there is still an underrepresentation of non-binary and third gender members contracted in 2022 and 2023, even seeing a decrease in 0.4% from 2016–2019 (2.0%) to 2023 (1.6%).

figures.finding: In the top 100 films of 2024, the female share of speaking characters falls with age: 45.1% of 0-12-year-olds, 54.6% of 13-20, 37.6% of 21-39 and 23.8% of those 40 or older; across 2007-2024 women were 24% of characters 40 or older.
figures.applies: US/North American theatrical film, top 100 domestic-grossing narrative films, 2024 (40+ series 2007-2024); apparent age.
figures.use: The film parts written for a player's playing age and Billed As: an Actress over 40 meets about one part in four of those written for her age band, an Actor three in four.

sources.said: In terms of speaking characters’ age, gender balance was observed in 2024 with 0-to 12-year-olds (males=54.9%, females=45.1%) and 13- to 20-year-olds (females=54.6%, males=44.8%). Turning to 21- to 39-year-olds, women only accounted for 37.6% of all speaking roles. The results were even more problematic for women 40 years of age or older. Here, women only accounted for 23.8% of older characters.
Total 76% 24%

figures.finding: In the top 100 US films of 2025, 28% of major female characters were 40 or older against 59% of major male characters; women 60 and older were 2% of major female characters and men 60 and older 8% of major male characters.
figures.applies: US theatrical film, top 100 domestic-grossing films of 2025.
figures.use: Within each Billed As, the age distribution of major film parts: an Actress's parts peak in her 30s and halve in her 40s; an Actor's grow into his 40s.

sources.said: The percentage of major female characters dropped precipitously from 32% in their 30s to 15% in their 40s. In stark contrast, the percentage of major male characters increased as they aged from their 30s (22%) to their 40s (29%). Just 28% of major female characters were 40 and older, whereas 59% of males were 40+.
accounting for just 2% of all major female characters. Men aged 60 and older comprised 8% of all major male characters.

figures.finding: On US broadcast and streaming series of 2025-26, 38% of major female characters were in their 30s but 15% in their 40s, while male characters went from 30% in their 30s to 28% in their 40s.
figures.applies: US broadcast and streaming original series, 2025-26.
figures.use: Television keeps the same age cliff for an Actress at 40 that film has.

sources.said: On broadcast and streaming programs, 38% of females were in their 30s but 15% were in their 40s. In contrast, the percentage of male characters declined only slightly from their 30s (30%) to their 40s (28%).

figures.finding: In UK television, people over 50 made 21% of scripted on-screen contributions (13% of Lead Actor, 23% of Supporting Actor, 32% of Background Actor contributions) against 47% of the national population.
figures.applies: UK television, Diamond 2025 reporting year (programmes broadcast 1 April 2025 to 31 March 2026).
figures.use: UK parts for a player over 50 are mostly supporting and background: a lead is rarer the older the playing age.

sources.said: On scripted shows, over-50s make far fewer contributions as Lead Actor (13%) than in Supporting Actor (23%) or Background Actor (32%) roles
Over-50s are much more highly represented on non-scripted (36%) shows than scripted (21%) ones

figures.finding: Of main characters in Australian TV drama 2016-2021, 62% were aged 18-44, 6.7% were 60 or over (23% of the population) and 2.2% were under 12 (15% of the population).
figures.applies: Australian TV drama, main characters, 2016-2021.
figures.use: Australian main parts by playing age: most fall between 18 and 44; few are written for 60 and over or for children.

sources.said: we found main characters tended to be younger people, with 62% of characters aged 18–44 years old.
Conversely, main characters under‑represent older adults: 6.7% were 60 years and over, much lower than this group’s share of the population (23%)
2.2% were under 12 years old, compared to the population benchmark of 15%.

figures.finding: Spotlight (UK) requires every performer to list a playing age range; it warns when the range is more than 15 years wide, suggests the actual age plus and minus five years as a rule of thumb, and keeps a young performer's range tight (e.g. 9-11 at ten).
figures.applies: Spotlight performer profiles (UK and Ireland casting platform), as published in 2026.
figures.use: The player's playing age is a range around the real age (default five years either side, at most fifteen wide, narrow for a child), and a part is open to the player when its age band overlaps that range.

sources.said: Your playing age means the range of ages that you can convincingly play as an actor and is mandatory information that must be on your Spotlight profile.
A warning message will appear if you select ages more than 15 years apart.
If you’re unsure what your playing age is, it’s recommended that you add and subtract five years from your actual age. For instance, if you’re 25, your playing age could be between 20 and 30.
Generally, it will sit tightly either side of their actual age, e.g. If they’re ten, it would be ‘9-11’.

figures.finding: Equity (UK) advises that performers should not be asked their age, ethnicity and other protected characteristics in a casting, except actual age when casting children or age-restricted advertising; a performer asked their age may give their playing range.
figures.applies: UK castings, auditions and interviews (Equality Act 2010; Equity's casting questions card and Casting Manifesto with Spotlight, CDG and PMA).
figures.use: In UK castings the game reads the player's playing range, never the real age, except for a child performer or an age-restricted advertisement.

sources.said: If asked about age, for example, you could say: "My playing range is..." Or "Equity advises me not to answer that"

Performers must not be asked for personal information, verbally or in writing prior to or during the audition process. This includes but is not limited to address, personal phone numbers, ethnicity and age except where actual age can and must be identified when casting children and in relation to casting for age restricted products in advertising.

figures.finding: Of 3,714 US television breakdowns (2017), 33.9% said 'open ethnicity' (please submit all ethnicities) and 30% gave no ethnicity; the rest named one: White 15.5%, Black 8.5%, Latina/o 8.3%, Asian 3.8%, Middle Eastern 1.6%, Indian/South East Asian 1.5%, Mixed Race/Biracial 1.4%, Pacific Islander 0.7%, Native American 0.5% (the published shares sum to 105.7%; the paper does not say why).
figures.applies: US scripted English-language television breakdowns (Breakdown Services), January-August 2017.
figures.use: About a third of US TV breakdowns name an ethnicity, and only those read the player's race or ethnicity; an open or silent breakdown reads nothing.

sources.said: Figure 2 shows the race/ethnicity of the Breakdowns as White 15.5% (n = 577), Black 8.5% (n = 316), Asian 3.8% (n = 144), Indian/South East Asian 1.5% (n = 59), Latina/o 8.3% (n = 309), Native American 0.5% (n = 20), Middle Eastern 1.6% (n = 62), Pacific Islander 0.7% (n = 28), Mixed Race/Biracial 1.4% (n = 52), No Ethnicity Given 30% (n = 1,115), Open Ethnicity
Open Ethnicity refers to a note in some Breakdowns that say “please submit all ethnicities.”
34.3% of Breakdowns for female characters stated “open ethnicity” (n = 483).

figures.finding: Every project on Breakdown Services carries a standard statement asking agents to submit performers without regard to race, ethnicity, age and other protected bases 'unless otherwise specifically indicated'; many breakdowns still specify race or ethnicity.
figures.applies: US breakdowns distributed by Breakdown Services (Breakdown Express, Actors Access), as observed 2017.
figures.use: The default for a part is open to every ethnicity; a part reads the player's race or ethnicity only where its breakdown names one.

sources.said: Paradoxically, every project listed in the Breakdowns includes the following statement: “We are committed to diverse, inclusive casting. For every role, please submit qualified performers, without regard to disability, race and ethnicity, age, color, national origin, or any other basis prohibited by law unless otherwise specifically indicated.” That said, many Breakdowns clearly do specify the race/ethnicity, age, gender, and so forth, of a role.

figures.finding: Of all US feature-film breakdowns from June to August 2006, 45.2% specified a race (5.4% through code words for white); 22.5% white, 8.1% black, 5.2% Latino, 4.3% Asian American, 0.5% Native American, 1.7% Middle Eastern, 2.9% a combination; 8.5% were 'open to all ethnicities'.
figures.applies: US feature-film breakdowns, 1 June to 31 August 2006.
figures.use: Film breakdowns name an ethnicity a little under half the time; the rest are open or silent.

sources.said: My analysis revealed that 45.2% of the listings specified a particular race, including 5.4% that used racial code words signifying to the average reader that the role was intended for a white actor.
A total of 22.5% of the listings identified the race as white; 8.1% identified the character as black; 5.2% as Latino; 4.3% as Asian American; and .5% as Native American.
In addition, 2.9% of the listings indicated the role was for a combination of races (such as for blacks and Latinos), and 1.7% indicated the role was for actors of Middle Eastern descent.

figures.finding: Of 3,803 speaking characters coded for apparent race or ethnicity in the top 100 films of 2024, 63.6% were white, 13.5% Asian, 13.2% Black, 4% multiracial, 3.1% Hispanic/Latino, 1.3% MENA, under 1% each American Indian/Alaskan Native and Native Hawaiian/Pacific Islander; 25% of leads or co-leads were from underrepresented groups.
figures.applies: US/North American theatrical film, top 100 films of 2024.
figures.use: The outcome side of US film casting by apparent race or ethnicity, to set how often a breakdown names each group; never a measure of the player.

sources.said: Of the 3,803 speaking or named characters that were coded for apparent race/ethnicity, 63.6% were white, 13.2% Black, 3.1% Hispanic/Latino, <1% American Indian/Alaskan Native, 13.5% Asian, <1% Native Hawaiian/Pacific Islander, 1.3% Middle Eastern/North African (MENA), and 4% multiracial/multiethnic.
Only 25% of all leads/co leads were from underrepresented backgrounds in 2024.

figures.finding: In 2025 US streaming films, BIPOC actors were 43.1% of all actors and 36% of leads (BIPOC were 45.2% of the US population).
figures.applies: US streaming films of 2025.
figures.use: Outcome share for US streaming film casting by race; context for the breakdown shares.

sources.said: Among total actors, BIPOC creatives ended up close to proportionate representation (43.1 percent).
Less than 2 to 1 among streaming film leads (36 percent)

figures.finding: In UK television, people from Black, Asian and minority ethnic groups made 36% of scripted on-screen contributions and 20% of non-scripted (23% of all on-screen; 17.5% of the population).
figures.applies: UK television, Diamond 2025 reporting year.
figures.use: UK scripted television's casting outcome by ethnicity; context only.

sources.said: This is slightly higher than national population estimates (17.5%; Annual Population Survey). Representation is much higher in scripted (36%) rather than in non-scripted (20%) roles

figures.finding: Of main characters in Australian TV drama 2016-2021, 71% were represented as Anglo-Celtic (53% of the population), 4.7% European (18%), 16% non-European (25%) and 7.2% First Nations.
figures.applies: Australian TV drama, main characters, 2016-2021.
figures.use: Australian casting outcome by cultural background; context only.

sources.said: While 53% of the Australian population have Anglo‑Celtic ancestry (for example, English, Irish, Scottish or Welsh), 71% of main characters in our current study of TV drama were represented as Anglo‑Celtic
the share of non‑European main characters (for example, those with Indian, Chinese or Middle Eastern ancestry) has more than doubled from 6.9% to 16%.
Among main characters in TV dramas between 2016 and 2021, 7.2% were First Nations

figures.finding: SAG's Casting Data Reports: non-Caucasian actors filled 29.3% of all TV and theatrical roles in 2007 and 27.5% in 2008.
figures.applies: US film and television roles under SAG's TV/Theatrical contracts, 2006-2008 (producers' hiring data).
figures.use: The union's last published outcome count by ethnicity; context only.

sources.said: 29.3 percent ofall TV and theatrical roles were filled bynon-Caucasian actors. In 2008, however, the numbers fell to 27.5 percent, slightly belowthe 2006 number of27.7 percent.

figures.finding: On US Equity stage contracts, BIPOC members received 30.26% of new contracts in 2023.
figures.applies: US professional stage (Actors' Equity Association), 2023 new contracts; self-reported.
figures.use: Stage casting outcome by ethnicity; context only.

sources.said: with 30.26% of all new contracts going to BIPOC members (an increase of 8.96% from the 2016–2019 collective seasons)

figures.finding: Published practice in the UK: performers must not be asked their ethnicity in a casting, and the Equity Casting Manifesto (with Spotlight, the CDG and the PMA) asks that an advertised breakdown be presented in the most inclusive way possible; in Canadian advertising the CMA asks a casting to say if it is open to all ethnicities and to list the ethnicities wanted rather than 'ethnically ambiguous'.

value.canada_advertising_rule: say if open to all ethnicities; list specific ethnicities

figures.applies: UK castings (Equity and Spotlight, 2026); Canadian advertising castings (Canadian Marketing Association DEI Committee, May 2023).
figures.use: Nobody in a casting asks the player's ethnicity; a breakdown that names an ethnicity is matched against the player's own optional field, and the game never infers it.

sources.said: Where roles are advertised, the casting breakdown should be presented in the most inclusive way possible.

In line with the law and with specific exceptions, performers should not be asked for personal information, verbally or in writing, as part of the audition. This includes actual age, ethnicity, disability, pregnancy, marital/civil partnership status or sexual orientation.
Specify if the casting is open to all ethnicities. List all who may attend rather than being generic.
Keep age as broad as possible, e.g., adult, child or looks like 40-70 year-old.

figures.finding: Of 8,798 films released in North American cinemas 2003-2017, 81.4% featured English as a main language and 31% had more than one language; French featured in 12%, Spanish 8.6%, German 5.2%, Hindi 4.9% (a film counts if it has at least a line in the language).
figures.applies: Films released in North American cinemas, 2003-2017; counts films, not roles.
figures.use: A film in the North American market has a second language about three times in ten; only such a film can write a part asking a language other than English. The share of parts (not films) is not published (see blockers).

sources.said: Across those 8,798 movies studied, 81.4% featured English as one of their main languages. Other popular languages included French (featured in 12% of movies), Spanish (8.6%), German, (5.2%) and Hindi (4.9%).
Films can have more than one language, and indeed, 31% of the films in my study did.

figures.finding: The main US television breakdowns distributed to Los Angeles and New York agents are English-language; Spanish-language network characters (Telemundo) were not in them in 2017.
figures.applies: US SAG-AFTRA television breakdowns, 2017.
figures.use: A US market part assumes English; a part in another language belongs to that language's market and reads the player's languages.

sources.said: This study examines English language television shows. While Telemundo is in negotiations with SAG-AFTRA (McNary, 2018), Telemundo characters are not currently included in the main Breakdowns distributed to LA and NY agents and managers.

figures.finding: Academy Awards (99th, films of 2026, ceremony 2027): acting is split by sex, Actor and Actress in Leading and Supporting Role; members of the Actors Branch decide lead or supporting on the ballot; only credited roles performed by consenting humans are eligible; no rule for a non-binary performer is stated.

categories: Performance by an actor in a leading role
Performance by an actor in a supporting role
Performance by an actress in a leading role
Performance by an actress in a supporting role

figures.applies: 99th Academy Awards rules (document dated June 2026), films of 2026.
figures.use: An Oscar-eligible performance competes as Actor or Actress by the player's Billed As.

sources.said: ACTING: Performance by an actor in a leading role. Performance by an actor in a supporting role. Performance by an actress in a leading role. Performance by an actress in a supporting role.
Only roles credited in the film’s legal billing and demonstrably performed by humans with their consent will be considered eligible.
The determination as to whether a role is a leading or supporting role shall be made individually by members of the branch at the time of balloting.

figures.finding: BAFTA Film Awards: the four acting categories are split, Leading Actor, Leading Actress, Supporting Actor and Supporting Actress; for directing, the longlist includes directors who identify as non-binary; BAFTA's rule for a non-binary performer was not reached (see blockers).
figures.applies: EE BAFTA Film Awards, 2025 rules (key changes published September 2024).
figures.use: A BAFTA performance competes as Actor or Actress by Billed As.

sources.said: the Acting chapter vote will vote for up to their top ten ranked, of which the first seven in the longlists for Leading Actor, Leading Actress, Supporting Actor and Supporting Actress will be automatically longlisted.

the top women and men directors, directors who identify as non-binary and mixed-gender directing teams (within the voting results range of the top 10 women and men directors) will be longlisted to a maximum of 11, with gender parity upheld between women and men directors.

figures.finding: Golden Globes (84th): acting is split into Female Actor and Male Actor categories in film and television; the studio or publicist picks the category (male actor vs. female actor) and the Eligibility and review committees can change it by a two-thirds vote; no rule for a non-binary performer is stated.

value.category_chosen_by: studio or publicist, reviewable by committee (two-thirds)

figures.applies: 84th Annual Golden Globes Eligibility and Consideration Rules (3 August 2026).
figures.use: A Globe entry is placed Female or Male Actor by the player's Billed As.

sources.said: The studio or publicist submitting a motion picture or television program initially selects the award categories for which it is entered (e.g., male actor vs. female actor, drama vs. musical/comedy or lead vs. supporting).
Best Performance by a Female Actor in a Motion Picture – Drama

figures.finding: The Actor Awards presented by SAG-AFTRA (33rd): individual categories are split, Male Actor and Female Actor, in film and television; the submission names its category and the Awards Committee may review placement; no gender rule is written.
figures.applies: 33rd Annual Actor Awards Presented by SAG-AFTRA, rules for 2026 performances (submissions close 2 November 2026).
figures.use: An Actor Awards submission enters Male or Female Actor by the player's Billed As.

sources.said: Outstanding Performance by a Male Actor in a Leading Role Outstanding Performance by a Female Actor in a Leading Role
The Actor Awards reserves the right to have all category placement reviewed by the Awards Committee.

figures.finding: Primetime Emmys (78th): acting categories are titled Actor and Actress; a nominee in any category titled Actor or Actress may ask for 'Performer' on the nomination certificate in place of Actor or Actress (the rule dates from 2021).

value.nonbinary_rule: nominee may request 'Performer' on the certificate

figures.applies: 78th Emmy Awards 2025-2026 Rules and Procedures (Version 4, 7 April 2026).
figures.use: An Emmy entry is Actor or Actress by Billed As; a nominee may be named Performer on the certificate.

sources.said: Performer nominees in any performer category titled “Actor” or “Actress” may request that their nomination certificate carry the term “Performer” in place of Actor or Actress.
Category 62 OUTSTANDING LEAD ACTRESS IN A DRAMA SERIES

figures.finding: Tony Awards (2025-26): eight acting categories split Actor and Actress (Leading and Featured, Play and Musical); the Administration Committee decides category placement and its decision cannot later be changed; a non-binary performer's category is in practice left to the performer (Cole Escola in Leading Actor in a Play, 2025).
figures.applies: The Tony Awards Rules and Regulations 2025-2026; practice reported for the 2023 and 2025 seasons.
figures.use: A Tony entry is Actor or Actress by Billed As; a non-binary player chooses.

sources.said: Best Performance by an Actor in a Leading Role in a Play Best Performance by an Actress in a Leading Role in a Play
Once the placement of an eligible candidate in a category has been decided by the Tony Awards Administration Committee, the placement cannot be changed at a later date.

J. Harrison Ghee and Alex Newell became the first non-binary actors to win acting Tony Awards in 2023, both competing in male actor categories. The designation is typically left up to the actor to decide.

figures.finding: Olivier Awards (2026): acting awards are split, Best Actor, Best Actress and their Supporting and Musical counterparts; no rule for a non-binary performer was found.
figures.applies: Olivier Awards 2026 (ceremony 12 April 2026), Society of London Theatre.
figures.use: An Olivier entry is Actor or Actress by Billed As.

sources.said: Jack Holden received the highly competitive Best Actor award for his performance in Kenrex
The coveted Best Actress award was won by Rosamund Pike

Silver Bear for Best Supporting Performance

figures.finding: Gotham Awards: from 2021 the acting awards are gender-neutral, Outstanding Lead Performance and Outstanding Supporting Performance replacing Best Actor and Best Actress (announced 5 August 2021).

figures.finding: Film Independent Spirit Awards: gender-neutral Best Lead Performance and Best Supporting Performance in film and television, announced 23 August 2022 for the 2023 awards; the 2027 rules keep Best Lead/Supporting/Breakthrough Performance.
figures.applies: Film Independent Spirit Awards, 2023 ceremony onward (2027 rules current).
figures.use: A Spirit Award performance competes regardless of Billed As.

sources.title: USC Annenberg Inclusion Initiative, Inequality in 1,800 Popular Films (2025)
sources.basis: USC Annenberg Inclusion Initiative's own content analysis of the 100 top-grossing domestic narrative films each year, 2007-2024
sources.said: Gender. 4,401 speaking or named characters were coded across the 100 top-grossing movies of 2024. Of these characters, 66.2% were male, 33.6% were female, and <1% (.18) were non-binary. … The percentage of films with a female protagonist (lead/co lead) was at a historic high in 2024 (55%). … In terms of speaking characters’ age, gender balance was observed in 2024 with 0-to 12-year-olds (males=54.9%, females=45.1%) and 13- to 20-year-olds (females=54.6%, males=44.8%). Turning to 21- to 39-year-olds, women only accounted for 37.6% of all speaking roles. The results were even more problematic for women 40 years of age or older. Here, women only accounted for 23.8% of older characters. … Total 76% 24% … Of the 3,803 speaking or named characters that were coded for apparent race/ethnicity, 63.6% were white, 13.2% Black, 3.1% Hispanic/Latino, <1% American Indian/Alaskan Native, 13.5% Asian, <1% Native Hawaiian/Pacific Islander, 1.3% Middle Eastern/North African (MENA), and 4% multiracial/multiethnic. … Only 25% of all leads/co leads were from underrepresented backgrounds in 2024.

sources.title: Center for the Study of Women in Television and Film (San Diego State University), It's a Man's (Celluloid) World 2025
sources.basis: the Center's own coding of every character seen speaking at least one line in the top 100 domestic-grossing films
sources.said: The percentage of female characters in speaking roles increased slightly to 38% in 2025, up 1 percentage point from 37% in 2024. The percentage of major female characters declined 3 percentage points, from 39% in 2024 to 36% in 2025. … The percentage of major female characters dropped precipitously from 32% in their 30s to 15% in their 40s. In stark contrast, the percentage of major male characters increased as they aged from their 30s (22%) to their 40s (29%). Just 28% of major female characters were 40 and older, whereas 59% of males were 40+. … accounting for just 2% of all major female characters. Men aged 60 and older comprised 8% of all major male characters.

sources.title: Center for the Study of Women in Television and Film (SDSU), Boxed In 2025-26
sources.basis: the Center's own coding of over 2,500 characters in one randomly selected episode of each series
sources.said: In 2025-26, females accounted for 44% (44.2%) of all speaking characters on broadcast network and streaming programs. This represents a decline of 2 percentage points from 46% in 2024-2025. Males comprised 56% (55.7%), and transgender characters less than one half of 1% (0.1%) of speaking characters … In 2025-26, females comprised 46% (46.3%) of all speaking characters appearing on broadcast network programs. … In 2025-26, females accounted for 43% (43.0%) of all speaking characters on streaming programs. … On broadcast and streaming programs, 38% of females were in their 30s but 15% were in their 40s. In contrast, the percentage of male characters declined only slightly from their 30s (30%) to their 40s (28%).

sources.title: Lauren Alexandra Sowa, Breaking Stereotypes or Stereotypical Breakdowns?, International Journal of Communication 15 (2021) 3358-3378
sources.basis: peer-reviewed textual analysis of the Breakdown Services breakdowns for the 2017 casting season
sources.said: Figure 1 shows the gender distribution in the Breakdowns as Men 57.6% (n = 2,141), Women 37.9% (n = 1,408), Open Gender … Open Gender means casting is open to either a man or woman in the role. … Figure 2 shows the race/ethnicity of the Breakdowns as White 15.5% (n = 577), Black 8.5% (n = 316), Asian 3.8% (n = 144), Indian/South East Asian 1.5% (n = 59), Latina/o 8.3% (n = 309), Native American 0.5% (n = 20), Middle Eastern 1.6% (n = 62), Pacific Islander 0.7% (n = 28), Mixed Race/Biracial 1.4% (n = 52), No Ethnicity Given 30% (n = 1,115), Open Ethnicity … Open Ethnicity refers to a note in some Breakdowns that say “please submit all ethnicities.” … 34.3% of Breakdowns for female characters stated “open ethnicity” (n = 483). … Paradoxically, every project listed in the Breakdowns includes the following statement: “We are committed to diverse, inclusive casting. For every role, please submit qualified performers, without regard to disability, race and ethnicity, age, color, national origin, or any other basis prohibited by law unless otherwise specifically indicated.” That said, many Breakdowns clearly do specify the race/ethnicity, age, gender, and so forth, of a role. … This study examines English language television shows. While Telemundo is in negotiations with SAG-AFTRA (McNary, 2018), Telemundo characters are not currently included in the main Breakdowns distributed to LA and NY agents and managers.

sources.title: Russell K. Robinson, Casting and Caste-ing: Reconciling Artistic Freedom and Antidiscrimination Norms, 95 California Law Review 1 (2007)

Fifty-nine percent of the roles were designated male roles, and 35% were designated female. … My analysis revealed that 45.2% of the listings specified a particular race, including 5.4% that used racial code words signifying to the average reader that the role was intended for a white actor. … A total of 22.5% of the listings identified the race as white; 8.1% identified the character as black; 5.2% as Latino; 4.3% as Asian American; and .5% as Native American. … In addition, 2.9% of the listings indicated the role was for a combination of races (such as for blacks and Latinos), and 1.7% indicated the role was for actors of Middle Eastern descent.
